candidates.title: Trajectory fit alone does not identify causal edges: a white-box masked ODE benchmark for trans-omics digital twins of drug action mechanisms
candidates.abstract: Dynamic multi-omics models infer drug mechanisms from trajectories, but trajectory accuracy alone cannot verify that learned regulatory edges are mechanistically correct. We asked to what extent fitting time-series dynamics identifies intervenable causal edges across observation and optimization budgets.We built white-box ordinary differential equations with candidate-edge masks for gene-expression, protein, signalling and metabolite dynamics, using a mouse-liver trans-omics topology and ground-truth semi-synthetic time series. Under noise-free,complete, densely sampled data, from-scratch training ranked edges near chance(edge-class area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve, 0.48-0.53); the unattainable oracle-initialized upper bound reached 0.94-0.99 on the same metric.Unobserved layers absorbed error. In ground-truth knockout tests, development-batch endpoint-sign accuracy was 67.9% for one-hop non-convergent targets but 33.3% for two-hop targets. Across tested practical budgets, fitting did not yield reliable edge recovery; trajectory fit alone therefore does not establish mechanistic identification. This benchmark supports mechanistic audits and exploratory per-prediction confidence grading in multi-omics models.

candidates.title: Comparative Mitogenomics and Molecular Phylogeny of Agriculturally Significant Tephritid Fruit Fly Pests in Bangladesh
candidates.abstract: Tephritid fruit flies of the tribe Dacini rank among the most economically destructive agricultural pests globally, with several species of Bactrocera Macquart and Zeugodacus Hendel causing severe losses to fruit and vegetable production across South and Southeast Asia. Bangladesh harbors several economically important dacine species, including Bactrocera dorsalis (Hendel), B. carambolae (Drew & Hancock), B. zonata (Saunders), B. correcta (Bezzi) and Zeugodacus cucurbitae (Coquillett). Here we present a comparative mitogenomic and phylogenetic framework based on 21 unique GenBank mitogenome records: 19 dacine ingroup records and two outgroups. The ingroup includes B. papayae, B. philippinensis and B. invadens, whose synonymy with B. dorsalis is disputed. All records contained 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs) and two rRNA genes. Genome size in the 14 taxa of subgenus Bactrocera ranged from 15,273 to 15,977 bp. Whole-genome AT content ranged from 66.6% in B. tsuneonis to 82.2% in Drosophila melanogaster, and the five focal pest species clustered at 72.9-73.6%. Maximum-likelihood analysis of a 13,600-site alignment (13 PCGs plus 12S and 16S rRNA; GTR+FO; IQ-TREE v1.6.11; 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, UFBoot) recovered the B. dorsalis complex (UFBoot = 100), within which pairwise distances were only 0.64-1.33%, and a B. correcta + B. zonata pair (UFBoot = 100). Nine taxa showed compositional heterogeneity and third codon positions were highly variable, so deeper nodes should be interpreted cautiously. As no Bangladeshi specimens were sequenced, this study is a curated reference baseline for molecular identification and pest surveillance, not a population-genomic analysis.

candidates.title: Effects of different shading levels on growth, physiology and leaf surface micromorphology of Sorbus sibirica "Dong Hong" seedlings
candidates.abstract: Background: Shading may influence nursery cultivation of Sorbus sibirica "Dong Hong", but its growth and physiological responses remain insufficiently characterised. Aims: To assess seedling responses to shading and inform container nursery management. Methods: One-year-old potted seedlings were grown under full sunlight (CK) and nominal shading levels of 30% (L1), 50% (L2) and 70% (L3) for 100 days in Qiqihar, China. Growth, biomass allocation, root morphology, physiological traits and leaf micromorphology were assessed. Results: Seedling height, total biomass, chlorophyll and soluble protein contents peaked under L1, whereas basal diameter and invertase activity declined with increasing shade. Under L1, total root length and mean root diameter were comparable to CK, but root tip number and root volume were lower. Root biomass proportion remained similar across treatments. L2 and L3 had higher leaf biomass proportions but lower total biomass than CK. Shaded seedlings had smaller stomatal dimensions. Biomass and root morphological values were lowest under L3. Conclusions: L1 combined greater biomass with thinner stems and altered root morphology. Restricted rooting volume, limited environmental monitoring and a single summer-to-autumn trial warrant validation before extending these findings to other seasons, regions or cultivation systems.

candidates.title: Microbes use transporters to regulate the release of metabolites based on value
candidates.abstract: Microbial interactions are shaped by the exchange of metabolites, ranging from intermediates in central carbon metabolism to amino acids, vitamins and fermentation by-products. While specific metabolic processes such as overflow metabolism are well documented, a general principle explaining the chemical diversity of metabolite release and the variation in individual release rates remains elusive. Here, using a combination of computational and experimental approaches on seven different microbes, we show that release rates are negatively correlated with the value of metabolites, and that this relationship explains more variability in release rates than other frequently associated factors. By measuring metabolite release from 67 E. coli mutants lacking individual transport genes, we find that transporters both cause and counteract net metabolite release. These findings suggest that metabolite release constitutes a fitness cost that microbes have evolved to reduce, while revealing the underlying transport mechanism. This unifying explanation reshapes our understanding of how microbial interactions emerge and persist.

candidates.title: Identification of SAMD4B as a Centrosome-Associated Regulator of the Sonic Hedgehog Signaling Pathway
candidates.abstract: Background: Many protein-protein interactions are required for the assembly and function of primary cilia, microtubule-based organelles critical for the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway and, in turn, for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis. However, our understanding of this complex process remains incomplete. Methods: To identify new regulators of primary cilia formation or function, we carried out proximity labeling experiments and compared interactomes under ciliogenesis-restrictive and permissive conditions. Using an unbiased strategy, we selected candidates that were tested functionally by siRNA-mediated depletion or gene editing, in combination with gene expression analysis and various microscopy techniques, using either vertebrate cell lines or zebrafish as model systems. Results: We demonstrate that one of our identified candidates, protein SAMD4B, is associated with the centrosome and is required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish. Our data implicate defective ciliary recruitment of Shh pathway regulators ARL13B and SMO as a plausible mechanism underlying the SAMD4B-mediated regulation of Shh signaling. Conclusions: Together, our data identify a previously unrecognized link between SAMD4B, a protein known to be associated with cytoplasmic RNA condensates, and ciliary signaling.

candidates.title: Long-term population monitoring reveals an alarming decline in the endangered endemic Reunion Harrier Circus maillardi
candidates.abstract: Insular species are disproportionately vulnerable to extinction due to small population sizes, geographic isolation, and high susceptibility to stochastic and anthropogenic pressures. The Reunion Harrier Circus maillardi, the last breeding raptor on La Reunion (Indian Ocean), is currently listed as Endangered (EN) on the IUCN Red List, although population decline has so far only been suspected rather than robustly quantified. Concerns have recently emerged regarding the demographic impacts of secondary poisoning from anticoagulant rodenticides used for rat control in agricultural landscapes, in addition to habitat loss, fragmentation, and reduced genetic diversity. Here, we analysed data from three standardised island-wide breeding surveys (1998--2000, 2009--2010, 2017--2019), encompassing 346 sampling points and totalling over 1,500 h of observation, to quantify population trends and their spatial variation. Using generalized additive mixed models accounting for spatial structure and heterogeneous survey designs, we detected a significant decline of -46% [-62%; -27%] in the relative abundance of breeding pairs at the island scale over 21 years, equivalent to three generations, supporting the species' current Endangered status. The decline was steeper between 1998 and 2009 (-33% [-52%; -9%]) than between 2009 and 2017 (-18% [-42%;+14%]). The decrease was more markedly pronounced in the eastern part of the island (-57% [-71%; -40%]) than in the west (-29% [-53%; + 0.8%]), reflecting a complete reversal of the historical east-west abundance gradient. Combined with previous evidence of inbreeding, high mutational load, and rodenticide exposure, these results suggest the population is undergoing an extinction vortex requiring immediate, spatially targeted conservation actions, including reduced rodenticide exposure and genetic management. These findings also underscore the need for sustained monitoring and improved demographic knowledge to support the implementation of the ongoing National Species Action Plan

candidates.title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
candidates.abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

candidates.title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
candidates.abstract: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

candidates.title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
candidates.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

candidates.title: GEI-17-mediated SUMOylation of GDP dissociation inhibitor GDI-1 regulates apoptotic cell clearance
candidates.abstract: by Lei Yuan, Peiyao Li, Aiying Ma, Chao Li, Fuqiao Liu, Yunmin Xie, Qian Zheng, Hui Wang, Hui Xiao Apoptotic cell clearance represents the final stage of apoptosis and involves phagosome formation, maturation, and digestion. Here, we found that SUMO modifications participate in apoptotic cell clearance by influencing phagosomal degradation activity in C. elegans . The SUMO E3 ligase, GEI-17, SUMOylates GDP dissociation inhibitor (GDI-1) at K270 to trigger phagosomal degradation. Upon SUMOylation, GDI-1 facilitates release of GDP-bound RAB-1, which is subsequently converted to the GTP-bound form in a manner dependent on GDI displacement factor, PRAF-3. RAB-1 conversion enables binding and translocation of RAB-7 from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to promote phagosome maturation and degradation activity. In the absence of GDI-1 SUMOylation, GDI-1 binds to GDP-RAB-1, sequestering it in the cytoplasm, resulting in impaired phagosomal degradation. Furthermore, we found SUMOylation of GDI1 at a conserved site plays a crucial role in efferocytosis regulation in mammals. This study defines a previously unrecognized mechanism by which SUMOylation drives apoptotic cell clearance.

candidates.title: Local feedback governs cell fate transition to drive self-organized phenotypic equilibrium in hierarchical tumors
candidates.abstract: by Emma Legait, Charlotte Rulquin, Lauranne Bouteille, Raphaël Clément, Cédric Maurange How cell-state transitions are regulated along a tumor lineage to determine its overall cellular composition remains unclear. Using a simple hierarchical tumor model in Drosophila , we show that differentiation of cancer stem cells (CSCs) into transit amplifying progenitors (TAPs) depends on the fraction of TAPs among their immediate neighbors. This relationship is captured by a local feedback transition rule that quantitatively predicts CSC transition probability. Implementing this rule in 3D growth simulations spontaneously recapitulates CSC clustering and the emergence of a stable CSC fraction within tumors. Mechanistically, the local feedback is mediated by EGFR signaling from newly produced TAPs, propagating differentiation across CSC clusters. Consistently, we show that clustering protects the CSC pool from depletion driven by surrounding TAPs, indicating that spatial architecture and lineage dynamics are tightly coupled. Together, these findings show that a local feedback governing fate transitions drives emergent spatial organization that stabilizes the stem cell fraction in hierarchical tumors.

candidates.title: Migration as a key influence on ungulate eco-evolutionary history
candidates.abstract: by Gustavo Burin Species can overcome resource limitations by migrating to more favourable areas. A new study in PLOS Biology shows that migration has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, that likely led to changes in ecosystem functioning. Species can overcome environmental limitations by migrating to more favorable areas. This Primer explores a new study in PLOS Biology showing that this behavior has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, which in turn likely led to changes in ecosystem properties and functioning.

candidates.title: A specialized microbiome enriched in nitrification and halogen cycling potential resolved from multi-omics investigation of a Caribbean suboxic and acidic marine sinkhole.
candidates.abstract: Background The Luymes Sinkholes, located on the Luymes Bank northwest of Saba, represent a unique marine environment characterized by distinct biogeochemical gradients. Most noticeable is an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 Results We identified a distinct microbial community within the submerged acid lake different from the non-acidic sinkholes, with increased abundances of Nitrospinota, Thermoproteota, Planctomycetota, and Actinobacteriota. We also found three enriched classes of dissolved compounds within the submerged acid lake: (1) large, (2) low-polarity, and (3) halogenated metabolites, including iodides and halobenzoic acids. Correlations between microbial taxa and metabolite classes show potential links between nitrifying archaea and halogenated compound cycling. We further supported these findings using the functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and protein clusters showing enrichment of nitrification and halogen cycling genes, suggesting the presence of specialized degradation and biosynthetic pathways, directly connecting microbial metabolism to the observed geochemical conditions. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that the submerged acid lake contains specific microbially driven biogeochemical processes under acidified and low-oxygen conditions, providing a natural model for future extreme ocean acidification scenarios. With this multi‑omics approach, we were able to connect the microbial metabolism with this unique environment, thereby expanding our understanding of how both are interconnected. Video Abstract.

[Introduction]
Across all environments, microbes help sustain ecosystems by exchanging and transforming key elements such as nitrogen [31], carbon, and sulfur [65, 73], generating energy through chemo- or phototrophic metabolisms, and recycling nutrients. Consequently, microbes directly shape their environments by altering nutrient availability, and the composition and redox structure of the Dissolved Organic Matter (DOM) comprising the exometabolome [45, 67, 77]. In turn, microbial community composition and function are shaped by physicochemical conditions, including pH, oxygen availability, nutrient supply, and hydrodynamic connectivity [69], leading to a bidirectional relationship where each impacts the other. Comprehensive multi-omics studies, integrating metagenomics, metabolomics, and environmental measurements, are needed to resolve the intricate biogeochemical connections that shape the microbiome [31, 57, 79, 81]. Such multi-omics studies have been made possible the development of untargeted high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry of metabolomes [11] with advanced data processing tools [15, 27] and high-throughput metagenome shotgun sequencing [36, 38, 58] followed by de novo assembly and functional annotation [70]. These advances allow for increasingly detailed characterizations of potential microbe-metabolite interactions [42]. Despite these technological advances, the application of fully integrated multi-omics approaches in natural systems remains limited as the high complexity and natural variability of these systems introduce challenges that are largely absent from laboratory-based experiments [59]. Naturally stratified or physically isolated systems provide valuable opportunities to overcome some of these challenges by offering stable gradients over relatively small spatial scales [26]. Marine sinkholes can thus function as natural laboratories, as they often host sharp biogeochemical transitions.
Here, we characterize the microbial ecology of the northern sinkholes in the Luymes Bank, located at the northeast margin of the Saba Bank in the Caribbean Sea. Several of these sinkholes were previously described by Humphreys et al. [30], characterizing their complex geological origins and physical structure. Notably, Humphreys et al. [30] described an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 < 60 µmol/kg) submerged ‘lake’ starting at a depth of 220 m within the sinkhole with the deepest bottom depth (306 m). [Methods]
We collected a total of 59 paired metagenomic and metabolomic samples from 21 stations on the Luymes Bank near Saba in December 2019 (Fig. 1A). Water chemistry parameters were measured as described by [30] (Supplementary Methods, Supplementary Table S3). Based on these parameters samples were clustered using Ward’s minimal variance clustering into six environments as follows: surface (n = 16), platform (n = 12), shallow sinkhole (n = 14), deep sinkhole (n = 9), acid lake (n = 6), and mesopelagic (n = 2). More detailed information on sample collection and storage can be found in the Supplementary methods.
Characterization of the environment: A map of Luymes Bank and integrated sinkholes (modified from Humphreys et al. 2022). B Ward’s minimal variance clustering of physicochemical parameters; rows correspond to samples and are annotated by the six defined environmental clusters (surface (n = 16), platform (n = 12), shallow sinkhole (n = 14), deep sinkhole (n = 9), acid lake (n = 6), and mesopelagic (n = 2)). Before clustering all nutrients were log10 transformed and all factors were normalized using z-scores. C Sampling depths of samples grouped by sinkhole and area (FS = far south, E = east, S = south, W = west, N = north, and O = open ocean). Colored by environmental cluster, see B. D Boxplots of measured physicochemical parameters grouped and colored by environmental cluster, see legend in B
Flow cytometric enumeration of prokaryotes (including bacteria and archaea) and viruses was performed at the NIOZ according to the protocol by Brussaard et al. [6] and using a TE buffer at pH 8.2. Samples were diluted in TE buffer and stained with the nucleic acid-specific green fluorescence dye SYBRGreen-I (10–5 dilution of commercial stock, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 15 min at room temperature for prokaryotes and for 10 min at 80 °C for viruses. Samples were then analyzed using a FACSCalibur flow cytometer with a 488 nm laser (BD Biosciences, USA).
Total DNA was extracted from seawater using the NucleoSpin Tissue DNA extraction kit following manufacturer instructions with some small adjustments (see supplementary methods section: “DNA isolation”). The isolated DNA was measured using the Denovix DS-11, and ranged from 1.7 to 12 ng/µL. [Results]
The Luymes Banks consist of a carbonate platform raised from the ocean floor, up to a depth of 60–80 m below the ocean surface and features multiple sinkholes with depths of up to 475 m below the ocean surface across their 66 km2 area [71]. We performed a characterization of seven of these sinkholes and adjacent open-ocean stations using multivariate clustering of hydrographic and biogeochemical parameters (phosphate, nitrate, nitrite, pH, depth, dissolved oxygen, transmissivity, salinity, and chlorophyll,(Fig. 1B, C). We excluded total alkalinity from the clustering analysis due to its strong collinearity with dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC, Supplementary Fig. S3). The multivariate clustering revealed six distinct environments: surface, platform, shallow sinkhole, deep sinkhole, acid lake, and mesopelagic (Fig. 1 C, D). Each cluster delineates a discrete physicochemical biome characterized by a unique combination of water column properties (Supplementary Fig. S3B), that approximately correspond to increasing depths (surface: n = 16, mean = 2.7 m, std = 3 m; platform: n = 12, mean = 70 m, std = 6 m, shallow sinkhole: n = 14, mean = 92 m, std = 10 m; deep sinkhole: n = 9, mean = 177 m, std = 47 m; acid lake: n = 6, mean = 275 m, std = 30 m; and mesopelagic: n = 2, mean = 536 m, std = 76 m). With the notable exception of the acid lake, the six different environments correspond to regular oceanographic patterns including higher nutrient levels in deeper, cooler water, and a chlorophyll max at intermediate depth [12, 40]. Samples collected near the surface (surface) were similar across all sinkholes and the open ocean, featuring high light, temperature, and dissolved oxygen with low concentrations of salinity, inorganic nutrients, and chlorophyll (Fig. 1C, D, E). Samples collected just above the platform depth at a depth of 60–80 m (platform), had higher salinity (mean = 37 ppt,std = 0.18 ppt) than the surface samples (mean = 34.7 ppt; std = 0.27 ppt), the highest chlorophyll concentrations of all environments (mean = 0.31 µg/kg, std = 0.03 µg/kg), and marginal increases in oxygen (+ 0.3 µmol/kg), nitrate (+ 0.11 µmol/kg), and nitrite (+ 0.035 µmol/kg) relative to the surface. The conditions within the sinkholes (shallow sinkhole, deep sinkhole, and acid lake) diverged from platform waters with increased salinity, nitrate, and phosphate. These patterns were consistent across both northern and southern sinkholes. The most striking deviations from the general p

[Discussion]
Exploring remote habitats has become more accessible thanks to large-scale omics datasets reducing the reliance on laboratory conditions. Yet these environments pose analytical challenges that differ markedly from those encountered in well-characterized or laboratory-controlled systems. A key difficulty lies in the holistic treatment of each sample: all detected metabolites and microbial taxa are jointly associated with the same environmental context, and consequently with one another. This obscures the directionality of causal relationships, as most conclusions are limited to co-occurrences, and our current analysis is primarily correlative. This limitation means that a mechanistic explanation is currently impossible to provide, based on the correlation network alone. Instead, the identified connections should be viewed as hypothesis-generating leads that warrant targeted validation through experiments or modeling. It is also reasonable to expect that aspects of microbial adaptation involve transcriptional changes or protein-level modifications and therefore are not captured in the functional abundance analysis. Further analysis such as protein sequence comparisons or RNA sequencing is likely to reveal additional fascinating insights within this ecosystem, if such data becomes available.
We can contemplate how our results relate to future ocean acidification. Laboratory studies report reduced nitrification rates under acidified conditions [5], yet the acid lake demonstrates that key nitrogen-cycling lineages can persist at pH levels of ~ 6 far below end-century surface ocean projections (~ 7.7–7.8). This suggests that at least some nitrifying archaea and bacteria possess sufficient plasticity to maintain function under chronic acidification. Cyanobacteria, which were still present at a low relative abundance within the nearly aphotic deep sinkholes (mean = 0.03, SD = 0.016), were almost completely lost in the acid lake (mean = 0.0017, SD = 0.0002), suggesting that, even when taking into account the low light conditions, photosynthetic primary producers may be more vulnerable to combined acidification and deoxygenation. Naturally, we should be careful with our interpretations, as the acid lake is nearly aphotic, higher in dissolved inorganic carbon and other nutrients, and resembles a chronically stressed, hydrodynamically isolated endpoint rather than the gradual transition expected in the open ocean,

candidates.title: Polaris: A toolkit for standardized construction, integration, and quantitative testing in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
candidates.abstract: Existing synthetic biology toolkits have expanded part libraries and assembly capabilities. However, new users may still encounter ambiguity in construct definitions, hierarchical transitions, genomic integration routes, and quantitative testing procedures. Here, we present Polaris, a Golden Gate toolkit for Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Polaris uses a MoClo-derived three-level hierarchy. Level 1 stores reusable parts, Level 2 generates transcription units and other intermediate constructs, and Level 3 supports multigene assembly and switching between testing and integration backbones. The toolkit distinguishes part interfaces from transcription unit interfaces, uses BpiI and BsaI in successive assembly stages, and provides parallel ccdB and mScarletI3 screening options. Integration modules and quantitative characterization frameworks were implemented in both hosts and demonstrated using representative genetic parts and activation and repression systems. A companion digital platform further encodes the Level 1 to Level 3 rules for assembly planning. Polaris connects hierarchical construction, stable genetic implementation, and quantitative testing within a common execution framework, providing a practical basis for data accumulation, part standardization, and future automation.

candidates.title: Cyborg bacteria as semi-living organelles for the augmentation of mammalian cells.
candidates.abstract: Synthetic organelles are engineered to replicate the compartmentalization and dynamic functionality of natural organelles, offering the potential to reprogram or rescue cellular functions. Existing approaches, such as protein cages, biomolecular condensates, and other artificial compartments, have shown promise but remain limited by their capacity to perform multifunctional tasks. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Cyborg Bacterial Organelles (CBOs), which are non-replicating, metabolically active bacteria engineered to function as living synthetic organelles within mammalian cells. Unlike synthetic systems or replicating endosymbionts, CBOs integrate the biological complexity of living organisms with the stability and tunability of engineered materials. CBOs are generated by permeating bacteria with poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEG) based monomers followed by intracellular UV induced hydrogel crosslinking, producing a structurally reinforced, non-replicative chassis capable of sustained activity inside host cells. Here, we show that CBOs remained detectable inside mammalian cells with substantially reduced morphological disruption compared with wild-type bacteria. Furthermore, we show that CBOs can perform complex functions intracellularly, including responses to extracellular chemical stimuli via synthetic gene circuits and execution of enzymatic reactions such as prodrug conversion into a therapeutic drug. Notably, we also show that CBOs protect host cells from chemically induced mitochondrial stress. Transcriptomic analysis revealed host gene expression changes associated with membrane remodeling, ion transport, and metabolic buffering, suggesting that CBOs modulate the host in protective and adaptive ways. Together, these findings establish CBOs as a novel hybrid material platform for intracellular engineering while addressing key limitations of current synthetic organelle systems. CBOs open new possibilities for cellular modulation in therapeutic and diagnostic applications.

candidates.title: ESCRT-III assembly restores membrane tension in micron-scale plasma membrane repair.
candidates.abstract: Plasma membrane integrity is essential for cellular survival, yet how cells repair micron-scale plasma membrane ruptures remains poorly understood. Here, using the genetically tractable Caenorhabditis elegans epidermis, we combine live imaging, genetics, super-resolution microscopy, and biophysical approaches to define a size-dependent role for endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT)-III in large-scale membrane repair. Small wounds induce transient, focal VPS-32 accumulation, whereas large wounds trigger the formation of a persistent but dynamic, circumferential ESCRT-III assembly that remains associated with the wound during repair. Formation of this assembly requires conserved ESCRT regulators, including ALX-1, TSG-101, and VPS-4, together with VPS-32 polymerization. The wound-associated ESCRT-III assembly is required for membrane tension restoration and efficient membrane repair, while disrupting VPS-32 polymerization impairs tension recovery, reduces vesicle recruitment and wound closure, and consequently compromises axon regeneration and organismal survival following injury. Together, our findings suggest that large plasma membrane wounds induce a persistent, dynamic ESCRT-III assembly that restores membrane tension and facilitates vesicle-mediated membrane addition to promote wound repair.

candidates.title: An engineered probiotic yeast converts extracellular ATP into adenosine to alleviate experimental colitis.
candidates.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic relapsing intestinal disorder characterized by mucosal inflammation, epithelial barrier disruption, and gut microbial dysbiosis. Excessive extracellular ATP (eATP) accumulates in inflamed intestinal tissues and amplifies immune activation through purinergic signaling, whereas adenosine generated from extracellular nucleotide metabolism exerts immunoregulatory effects. Here, we engineered the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii to sense eATP and convert it into adenosine through a CRISPR-engineered dual-enzyme pathway consisting of apyrase and 5'-nucleotidase. The engineered strain showed ATP-responsive pathway activation and efficiently generated adenosine from eATP, allowing extracellular nucleotide metabolism to be modulated in inflammatory settings. Oral administration of this strain significantly alleviated disease severity in acute dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis and showed beneficial effects in a repeated-DSS model, improved barrier-related epithelial features, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and supported mucosal recovery. Integrated microbiome and transcriptome analyses further showed partial restoration of gut microbial community structure, partial recovery of predicted microbial purine-related pathways, and attenuation of mucosal T-cell activation. Together, these findings indicate that engineered Saccharomyces boulardii can regulate extracellular purine metabolism in the inflamed gut and provide a microbial strategy for modulating intestinal inflammation.

candidates.title: From community profiling to functional insights: bacterial populations in marine sediments from an Antarctic Specially Protected Area (Terra Nova Bay, Ross Sea, Antarctica).
candidates.abstract: Marine sediments remain among the least characterised components of the Antarctic microbial landscape. Here, bacterial communities were investigated in sediments from three sites within the Antarctic Specially Protected Area No. 161, in Terra Nova Bay (Ross Sea, Antarctica). Samples were collected during the XXXIII Italian Antarctic Expedition. The sites differed in their local environmental context, including proximity to the Adélie penguin colony and Mario Zucchelli Station. Bacterial communities were characterised by 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V3-V4 region), with amplicon sequence variants resolved using DADA2, and complemented by PICRUSt2 predicted functional potential, bacterial isolation, and quorum-sensing bioassays. Bacteroidota and Proteobacteria dominated all sites, but community composition and diversity differed significantly among sampling sites. AC showed the highest alpha diversity, while ASPA2 showed the lowest. Of the 5423 amplicon sequence variants detected across the nine samples (three per site), 680 were shared across all samples and defined a core microbiome dominated by Bacteroidota and Proteobacteria. Despite marked differences in community composition, broad predicted functional profiles were relatively conserved, whereas finer-scale KEGG Orthology profiles showed site-associated variation. Seventeen psychrophilic strains were isolated, predominantly Psychrobacter, and most displayed hydrolytic activity towards olive oil, tributyrin, or both substrates. Biosensor-responsive activity was detected exclusively in enrichment cultures and not in extracts from individual isolates, providing preliminary evidence of putative quorum-sensing-related activity associated with mixed microbial consortia. These findings provide a baseline for investigating environmental drivers of Antarctic sediment microbiomes and microbial interactions in future studies.

candidates.title: Kidney-Alone Transplantation With siRNA Therapy in Primary Hyperoxaluria Type 1.
candidates.abstract: Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1) is a rare genetic disease causing severe hyperoxaluria, kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis, and progressive kidney failure (KF) followed by systemic oxalosis. Expert guidelines traditionally recommended liver-kidney transplantation (LKTx) for patients with vitamin B6-unresponsive PH1 and KF, with 1-year mortality of 5% to 15%. Small interfering ribonucleic acid (siRNA) therapies targeting hepatic oxalate production have shifted the treatment landscape. Eighteen patients on siRNA therapy with successful kidney-alone transplantion (KATx) have been reported. A multicenter, international, retrospective case series from 11 countries included patients with: (1) confirmed PH1 diagnosis; (2) KATx as definitive kidney replacement therapy; and (3) concurrent lumasiran and/or nedosiran treatment beyond the induction phase before and/or after transplantion. Thirty-eight patients were analyzed: at transplantion, 27 received lumasiran, 6 received nedosiran, and 1 received both; 60.5% carried a priori vitamin B6-responsive variants. All 25 AGXT alleles identified were pathogenic or likely pathogenic, including 3 not previously reported in PH1 and 1 requiring haplotype-level resolution. Median pretransplant plasma oxalate was 59 μmol/l (interquartile range [IQR], 30; range, 5-100). Donors were deceased in 57.9%; 39.5% of recipients were pediatric. Median follow-up was 25 months (range, 2-60). Peritransplant or posttransplant dialysis was used in 60.5%. Four patients diagnosed after KATx were included; 3 were successfully treated with lumasiran. One-year graft survival was 95%; patient survival was 100%. This international series supports KATx as standard of care for carefully selected patients with PH1 with assured long-term siRNA therapy and expert follow-up. Practical recommendations, including a peritransplant checklist emphasizing expert-centered care and vigilance for emerging complications, are provided.
authors: PH1NITx Working Group (PH1 Network for Investigating siRNA and Kidney Transplantation)55

candidates.title: Circular RNA: What they are, how they are formed, their function, and how we might be able to harness them for treatment of skin diseases.
candidates.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed circularly structured RNA molecules that influence cellular biology through multiple types of mechanisms. CircRNAs' most studied function is as a competitive endogenous RNA regulating microRNAs; however they can also interact with RNA binding proteins, regulate transcription, and encode proteins. In this review, we examine the role of circRNAs in skin diseases, including cancer, inflammatory skin diseases like psoriasis, and wound healing. Broader roles for circRNAs in diagnostics and therapeutics for skin diseases are also discussed.
